MRI: Magnetic Resonance Imaging: a scan that uses strong magnets and radio waves to create detailed images of organs and tissues.
CT scan: Computed Tomography scan: a series of X-ray images combined by a computer into cross-sectional views of the body.
ECG: Electrocardiogram: a test that records the heart's electrical activity to check rhythm and detect damage.
EKG: Electrocardiogram: a test that records the heart's electrical activity to check rhythm and detect damage.
BMI: Body Mass Index: weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared, a rough screen for healthy weight.
blood pressure: The force of blood pushing against artery walls, written as systolic over diastolic (e.g. 120/80 mmHg).
hypertension: Persistently high blood pressure, which raises the risk of heart disease and stroke.
hypotension: Abnormally low blood pressure, which can cause dizziness or fainting.
tachycardia: A resting heart rate faster than normal, generally over 100 beats per minute in adults.
bradycardia: A resting heart rate slower than normal, generally under 60 beats per minute in adults.
arrhythmia: An irregular heartbeat: too fast, too slow, or with an abnormal rhythm.
myocardial infarction: A heart attack: damage to heart muscle caused by a blocked blood supply.
anemia: A shortage of healthy red blood cells or hemoglobin, reducing oxygen delivery to the body.
diabetes: A chronic condition in which the body can't properly regulate blood sugar.
insulin: A hormone made by the pancreas that lets cells absorb glucose from the blood.
HbA1c: A blood test showing average blood sugar levels over roughly the past three months.
cholesterol: A waxy fat carried in the blood; high levels of certain types raise the risk of heart disease.
LDL: Low-Density Lipoprotein: often called 'bad' cholesterol, as high levels contribute to clogged arteries.
HDL: High-Density Lipoprotein: often called 'good' cholesterol, as it helps remove other cholesterol from the blood.
antibiotic: A medicine that kills or stops the growth of bacteria; it does not work against viruses.
antibody: A protein made by the immune system that recognizes and helps neutralize a specific invader.
antigen: A substance, often part of a germ, that triggers the immune system to produce antibodies.
mRNA: Messenger RNA: molecules that carry instructions from DNA for making proteins; also the basis of some vaccines.
immunotherapy: Treatment that helps the body's immune system fight diseases such as cancer.
chemotherapy: Treatment using drugs that kill fast-growing cells, most commonly used against cancer.
biopsy: Removing a small sample of tissue so it can be examined for disease.
benign: Not cancerous; a benign tumor does not invade nearby tissue or spread.
malignant: Cancerous; able to invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body.
metastasis: The spread of cancer from where it started to other parts of the body.
oncology: The branch of medicine that studies and treats cancer.
inflammation: The body's protective response to injury or infection, causing redness, heat, swelling, and pain.
autoimmune disease: A condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the body's own tissues.
placebo: An inactive substance or sham treatment used as a comparison in medical studies.
double-blind: A study design in which neither participants nor researchers know who receives the real treatment.
randomized controlled trial: A study that randomly assigns participants to a treatment or control group to test effectiveness.
RCT: Randomized Controlled Trial: a study that randomly assigns participants to treatment or control groups.
clinical trial: A research study in people that tests whether a medical treatment is safe and effective.
comorbidity: The presence of two or more health conditions in the same person at the same time.
prognosis: The likely course and outcome of a disease.
epidemiology: The study of how diseases spread and affect populations, and how to control them.
pathogen: A microorganism, such as a virus or bacterium, that can cause disease.
SSRI: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor: a common class of antidepressants that raise serotonin levels.
NSAID: Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug: pain relievers like ibuprofen that also reduce inflammation.
anesthesia: Medically induced loss of sensation or consciousness so procedures can be done without pain.
ICU: Intensive Care Unit: a hospital ward for patients with severe or life-threatening conditions.
CPR: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation: chest compressions and rescue breaths given when someone's heart has stopped.
sepsis: A life-threatening reaction in which the body's response to infection damages its own organs.
edema: Swelling caused by excess fluid trapped in the body's tissues.
idiopathic: Describes a disease that arises spontaneously or whose cause is unknown.
generic drug: A medication with the same active ingredient, dose, and effect as a brand-name drug, usually cheaper.
FDA: Food and Drug Administration: the U.S. agency that regulates the safety of food, drugs, and medical devices.
EHR: Electronic Health Record: a digital version of a patient's medical history shared across care providers.
HIPAA: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act: U.S. law protecting the privacy of health information.
telehealth: Healthcare services delivered remotely, such as video appointments with a doctor.
microbiome: The community of microorganisms, like bacteria, living in and on the body, especially the gut.
gene therapy: Treating disease by adding, replacing, or editing genes inside a patient's cells.
CRISPR: A gene-editing technology that can cut and modify DNA at precise locations.
DNA: Deoxyribonucleic acid: the molecule that carries the genetic instructions of living things.
PCR: Polymerase Chain Reaction: a lab technique that copies DNA many times, used in many diagnostic tests.
stem cells: Unspecialized cells that can develop into many different cell types in the body.
outpatient: Medical care that doesn't require an overnight hospital stay.
triage: Sorting patients by how urgently they need care.
